criterion.done_criterion: the baseline record exists and carries a worktree path, the pinned main SHA, a measured pass count and the name of every red test

stages.knowledge:
That this repository's canon is mutated only by sync-instructions-repo.sh and never by a

means.method:
The baseline must be a MEASUREMENT recorded to disk before any ref is touched, not a figure
carried over from the brief. The suite's known-red test is identified by name in the record,
so a later run can distinguish 'the same one test still fails' from 'a different test now
fails' — a bare count cannot make that distinction and so cannot support the regression
judgement stages 4-8 rest on. Refreshing the canonical checkout precedes measuring it, since a
baseline taken against a stale main describes a tree no later stage will ever observe.
means.procedure:
1. Run scripts/sync-instructions-repo.sh pull to refresh the canonical checkout and its remote refs.
2. Record main's resolved SHA as the `main_sha` line.
3. Run scripts/session-isolate.sh unlanded-branch-triage; capture its final stdout line (the workspace root) as the `worktree` line.
4. In the canonical checkout, run python3 -m pytest scripts/tests -q and record the summary counts as `baseline_passed` / `baseline_failed`.
5. Record each failing test's node id on its own `known_red` line.
6. Run scripts/verify-all.sh and record its pass/warn tally as `verify_all`.

stages.preconditions: The engine session is at an execution node, so the developer may write files at all.

principle.derivation:
The brief supplies that baseline as prose from an earlier session. Nine later stages in this
plan each need to answer 'did my landing break anything', and each would otherwise answer it

only form in which the comparison is checkable by anyone other than its author.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if the suite's failure set proves non-deterministic across runs at one SHA — then a
single pinned record is not a base at all and the regression control would have to become a
statistical one over repeated runs.
principle.source: The brief's own constraint paragraph, which reports the baseline as 4660 passed / 3 skipped / 1 failed with one named expected red.
principle.statement: A regression verdict is only as good as the base it is asserted against, so the base must be measured and written down before the first mutation, not reconstructed afterwards.

actor.capability_required: reading a git object database; writing the ledger under the plans directory

criterion.done_criterion: the ledger holds seventeen uniquely-named branch rows, each with a valid disposition, and every discard row names a patch-id command
criterion.verify_command: awk -F'\t' '!/^#/ && NF>=4 && $1!="main" {n++; if ($2 !~ /^(land|discard|file-as-task)$/) bad++; if (seen[$1]++) dup++; if ($2=="discard" && $3 !~ /cherry/) noprecond++} END {exit !(n==17 && bad==0 && dup==0 && noprecond==0)}' /Users/the0/.claude-agent/plans/unlanded-branch-triage-ledger.tsv

stages.knowledge:
That `git cherry` and `git log --cherry-mark` compute the same patch-id equivalence, and that
`git log --cherry-mark --right-only` is the form available here; that a three-dot diff
`main...origin/<b>` shows only branch-side changes since the merge base and therefore says
NOTHING about whether those changes also exist on main, so it must not be read as a landedness
signal; and that a git pathspec is cwd-relative.

means.means: git log --cherry-mark --right-only --oneline; git ls-remote --heads origin; git diff --name-only
means.method:
Landedness must be decided by PATCH-ID equivalence, never by commit subject. The discriminator
is `git log --cherry-mark --right-only --oneline main...origin/<branch>`, which marks each
commit `=` when an equivalent patch exists on main and `+` when none does; it therefore sees
through both a rebase (which changes the SHA) and a reword (which changes the subject), the two
transformations that defeat subject matching in opposite directions. The asymmetry of the
result must be respected rather than flattened: `=` is trustworthy evidence FOR discard, while
`+` is only the absence of an identical patch and never by itself proof that content is
missing, because a commit that landed squashed or conflict-resolved also reads `+`. So an
all-`=` branch may be dispositioned discard from this pass alone, and any branch with at least
one `+` may not be dispositioned discard here at all. Path arguments to git must be written
top-relative (`:(top)path` or a path from the repository root), because a pathspec resolves
against the caller's cwd and a subdirectory cwd silently turns a real path into a nonexistent
one, producing an empty diff that reads as 'no residual'.
means.procedure:
1. Enumerate the live remote branches with git ls-remote --heads origin and subtract main, so the domain comes from the remote rather than from the brief's table and carries no row for trunk itself.
2. For each, run git log --cherry-mark --right-only --oneline main...origin/<branch> and record the `=` and `+` counts.
3. Write a ledger row per branch: branch, disposition, precondition command, evidence.
4. Disposition all-`=` and zero-ahead branches as discard, citing the cherry-mark command as the precondition.
5. Disposition every branch carrying `+` commits as land or file-as-task, leaving the land-versus-file call for stages 6-8 where the rebase cost is visible.
6. For each branch with `+` commits, record its touched files (git diff --name-only main...origin/<branch>) in the evidence column, so stages 6-8 can order landings by file overlap.
7. Re-state in the ledger header which branches the brief's subject-match table mis-classified, so the correction is durable rather than buried in a reply.

stages.preconditions: A baseline record exists naming the pinned main SHA that every cherry-mark comparison is taken against.

principle.derivation:
The brief's subject-match table classifies that branch FULLY-LANDED-BY-REBASE on a 43-of-43
subject match, which is the strongest signal its method can emit; the patch-id test run on the
same refs finds five commits with no equivalent patch upstream. Since a discard acts on
exactly this verdict, the method that produced the stronger-looking answer would have deleted
five commits of work — so the measurement establishes not merely that the two methods differ
but that the cheaper one is wrong in the direction that loses data. Conversely the same test
confirms grant-merge-verbs genuinely landed (its one commit marks `=`, equivalent to 7fe9a4d),
so patch-id also supplies the positive evidence a discard needs.
principle.refutation:
Refuted for any commit that landed with modified content — squashed, partially applied, or
conflict-resolved differently — since its patch-id differs and it reads `+` though its content
is upstream. This is why `+` licenses no discard here and every `+` branch is adjudicated in
stages 6-8 instead.
principle.source:
Measured in this planning session against main=90a6f08: `git log --cherry-mark --right-only
--oneline main...origin/org-neutralize-core` returns 38 commits marked `=` and 5 marked `+`
(d754c76, 9dbca6e, a511f7d, 7f036c9, 633bd1e).
principle.statement: A verdict must be reached by a test that covers the ways its subject can vary; subject matching does not cover rebase or reword, and patch-id equivalence covers both.

subject.invariants:
No ref is created, moved or deleted by this stage — it is pure measurement. main stays at the
pinned SHA. The two branches measured at zero commits ahead are recorded, not silently dropped
for being uninteresting.
subject.material:
The seventeen remote branches of origin and their commits. Fifteen carry commits absent from
main by the brief's count; two — judge-import-blindness and solved-marker-007 — are absent
from the brief's inventory entirely and measured at zero commits ahead, making them stale refs
rather than unlanded work.
subject.result:
A tab-separated ledger holds one row per branch for all seventeen, each row carrying the
branch name, one of the three dispositions, the content-level command that established its
precondition, and the evidence that command produced. The rows for branches whose every
commit has an equivalent patch upstream say discard; the rows for branches carrying unique
commits say land or file-as-task. Nothing in the ledger rests on a commit-subject comparison.

means.means: curl against api.github.com with the token in ~/.github-token (the gh CLI is NOT installed here — measured exit 127); docs/adr/0005-activity-act-functional-places.md; the stage 2 ledger
means.method:
The defect set must be enumerated MECHANICALLY from the two authorities — a GET on /issues for
what is published and the ADR section for what was recorded — and then joined against the
ledger by the files each branch touches. Enumeration from either source alone is insufficient:
the ADR says what was found, the tracker says what was claimed, and only their join exposes a
claim that no longer matches the repository. A public issue's text may be contradicted only by
a branch whose fix is COMPLETE and tested; an unlanded partial attempt is not grounds for
telling the world a defect is fixed, and the reconciliation verdict must distinguish the two.
Every write to a public issue is an outward-facing act and is put to the user before it is
made, individually, with the exact comment text shown.
means.procedure:
1. GET /repos/sthe0/claude-agent-instructions/issues/N once per N in 73..82 with the ~/.github-token bearer, recording number, title, state and labels. Ten individual GETs rather than one list call, because a list call is subject to pagination and state filtering and could silently return nine of the ten, which is the one failure this enumeration must not have.
2. Read the eight-engine-defects section of docs/adr/0005-activity-act-functional-places.md and map each filed issue to the defect it records.
3. For each issue, search the ledger's evidence column for a branch touching the files that defect names.
4. For each candidate pair, read the branch's diff and decide whether its fix is complete and tested, or partial.
5. Write a row per issue: number, candidate branch (or none), verdict.
6. Draft one comment per falsified issue, naming the branch, its commit, and what the fix covers.
7. Put the drafted comments to the user for approval, then post the approved ones.
8. Record each posted comment's URL in the reconciliation row, and confirm by re-reading the issue that the comment is actually visible.

stages.preconditions: A ledger exists whose evidence column records, per branch, the files it touches — the join key this reconciliation needs.

principle.derivation:
The fix for the emphasis-marker defect is complete and tested on a branch while its issue is
published open, so the tracker asserts something the repository falsifies. Correcting the
claim needs only the observation that the branch exists — it is independent of the rebase,
review and user-gated push that landing requires, all of which can fail or be deferred. Two
acts of different cost and different failure modes are therefore separated, and the cheap
independent one is not held hostage to the expensive dependent one. Ordering it after landing
would leave the misleading claim standing for exactly as long as the landing takes.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if reading the branch shows the fix incomplete relative to what the issue describes —
then there is no false claim to correct, and the row's verdict records a partial attempt
instead.
principle.source: The brief's § Confirmed overlap paragraph, and commit 1560e3e's stat measured this session: 5 files, 237 insertions, including a new 150-line test_marker_emphasis.py.
principle.statement: A false outward-facing claim is corrected before the work that makes it true, because the claim misleads readers for as long as it stands and the correction does not depend on the fix.

landed, discarded or created. No org-internal identifier enters a public comment.

eight-engine-defects section, plus #82, the file-difficulty.py submit gate that is blind to

falsified by an unlanded branch, a comment saying so is visible on the issue itself. A reader
of the public tracker can no longer be misled into re-implementing a fix that already exists.

stages.conditions:
main is at the SHA the rebase was performed against at the moment of the push, so the
fast-forward precondition still holds; a competing landing in between invalidates it and the
rebase is redone. The user is present to answer the push gate. The suite's failure set after

criterion.done_criterion: origin/main contains the commit this stage delivered

stages.knowledge:
That land-branch.py is fast-forward-only and ref-only, refuses with exit 2 rather than forcing,
and deletes the remote branch, the local branch and the linked worktree as PART of landing
unless --keep-branch is passed; that no branch in this repository is currently
fast-forwardable, so a rebase is required before any landing; and that a commit hook must
never be bypassed with --no-verify.

means.means: git rebase in the isolated worktree; scripts/land-branch.py --check then land; python3 -m pytest
means.method:
The branch must reach a genuinely fast-forwardable state before landing, and it must reach it
by REBASE onto current main in the isolated worktree — not by a merge, and never by
hand-rolled checkout/reset/clean, since land-branch.py refuses rather than forces and the
canonical checkout is read-only to this session. Conflict is expected rather than exceptional:
main has moved on both scripts/lib/planner_plan_check.py and scripts/agentctl/dispatch.py
since this branch was cut, so a clean rebase is the surprising outcome and a conflicted one is
the normal path. The rebased result is tested before it is offered for landing, because a
rebase that resolves cleanly can still be semantically wrong. The push to main is put to the
user at the moment of the push, and landability is confirmed with --check first so the user is
answering a question whose mechanical half is already settled.
means.procedure:
1. In the isolated worktree, create a working branch at origin/marker-emphasis-tolerance.
2. Rebase it onto main, resolving conflicts in planner_plan_check.py and dispatch.py in favour of main's newer structure while preserving the emphasis-tolerance behaviour.
3. Run python3 -m pytest scripts/tests -q and compare the failure set against the stage 1 baseline record.
4. Run scripts/verify-all.sh and compare against the baseline tally.
5. Run scripts/land-branch.py --check --branch <working-branch> and read back the exact commands it would run.
6. Put the push to the user with the --check output as the evidence.
7. On approval, run scripts/land-branch.py --branch <working-branch>, which pushes to main and deletes the branch and its worktree.
8. Update the branch's ledger row to land, with the resulting main SHA and the literal token gate:approved as evidence, so the ledger records that a gate was actually held and not merely declared.
9. In the SAME user gate as the push, close the emphasis-defect issue with a closing comment naming the landed main SHA, and record the closure in the issues record's fourth column. The push and the closure are one decision because a landed fix and an issue still asserting the defect open are the same falsehood the stage exists to remove.

stages.preconditions: The public issue for this defect carries a reconciliation verdict, so landing closes a loop that has already been made visible rather than one nobody has been told about.

principle.derivation:
Every landing in this plan carries the same mechanical cost structure — rebase, test, gated
push — so cost does not order them. What differs is what each landing retires. This one is a
single commit, so its rebase risk is the lowest available, and it answers an issue the public
tracker currently states as open, so it is also the highest-value; the two normally-competing
criteria coincide here, which makes it first without a trade-off. The landing also converts the
stage 3 comment from a promissory note into a closable issue.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if the rebase onto main turns out to conflict irreducibly — if main's newer
planner_plan_check.py has already restructured the marker sites the fix depends on — in which
case this stops being the cheapest landing and is re-adjudicated with the heavyweights in
stage 8.
principle.source: scripts/land-branch.py's module docstring, read this session; and the cherry-mark measurement showing 1560e3e is the sole commit on the branch and marks `+`.
principle.statement: Among equally-valid orderings, the branch that discharges an outward-facing false claim is landed first, because its landing retires a published defect rather than only reducing a ref count.

The emphasis-tolerance behaviour the branch's tests pin survives the rebase unchanged. No
other branch's refs are touched. The canonical checkout's working tree is never mutated by
checkout, reset or clean. Comments are not added to the code the rebase touches.

main contains the emphasis-tolerance fix; the branch and its worktree are gone from origin and
from the local repository; the new test_marker_emphasis.py runs as part of the suite; and the
public issue that reported the defect can now be closed on the strength of trunk rather than of
a branch.

stages.conditions:

been pushed onto any of the three since they were measured. The user is available to authorize
the batch.

criterion.done_criterion: none of the three branch names resolves on origin any more
criterion.verify_command: git ls-remote --heads origin main | grep -q 'refs/heads/main$' || exit 1; test -z "$(git ls-remote --heads origin grant-merge-verbs judge-import-blindness solved-marker-007)"

stages.knowledge:
That a branch measuring zero commits ahead of main is fully merged and its ref is litter
rather than work; that `=` under cherry-mark means an equivalent patch is upstream even though
the SHA differs; and that a deletion built from an unguarded shell variable can collapse onto
an unintended target, so literal names are used.

means.means: git push origin --delete; git ls-remote --heads origin; git log --cherry-mark
means.method:
Each deletion is licensed individually by a re-run of the patch-id check at the moment of
deletion, not by the ledger row written earlier — main has moved since stage 2, and a check
whose result is read from a file records what was true then rather than what is true now. A
branch is deleted only when its every commit marks `=` or it is zero commits ahead; a single
`+` withdraws it from this stage and sends it to stage 8. Deletion is of the REMOTE ref by
name, with the literal name spelled out rather than interpolated from a variable, so an empty
expansion cannot widen the target.
means.procedure:
1. Re-run git log --cherry-mark --right-only --oneline main...origin/<branch> for each of the three, and confirm no `+` remains.
2. Confirm each ref's tip SHA still matches what stage 2 recorded, so nothing was pushed to it since.
3. Put the three deletions to the user as one batched decision, showing the per-branch evidence.
4. On approval, push an archive/<branch> tag at each ref's tip, with literal names, so the commit object stays reachable after the ref is gone.
5. Run git push origin --delete <branch> for each, with literal branch names.
6. Run git worktree list to confirm no linked worktree has the ref checked out; where one does, release that worktree first, then delete the corresponding local ref.
7. Record the deletion, its licensing evidence and the archive tag in each ledger row.

stages.preconditions: The ledger carries a patch-id verdict for each of these three branches, so the deletion is re-confirming an established finding rather than deciding one for the first time.

principle.derivation:
Deleting a remote ref is the one irreversible act in this plan — a landed branch can be
re-landed, but a deleted ref whose commits were not upstream is recoverable only from a
reflog that origin does not keep for the caller. The gap between stage 2's measurement and
this stage's action spans stage 4's landing, which moves main and therefore changes what
`main...origin/<b>` means. Re-running the check costs one command per branch; trusting the
recorded verdict costs the difference between a correct and an incorrect deletion, with no
mechanism in between to catch the error.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if origin is configured to retain deleted-branch refs recoverably (a server-side
reflog or protected-ref retention the caller can reach), which would make the deletion
reversible and the re-check merely tidy rather than load-bearing.
principle.source: Measured this session: grant-merge-verbs' commit 99d8a49 marks `=` against 7fe9a4d on main; judge-import-blindness and solved-marker-007 each return 0 from git rev-list --count main..origin/<branch>.
principle.statement: A destructive act re-establishes its own precondition at the moment it acts, because a precondition recorded earlier describes a state that may since have changed.

subject.invariants:
main is unchanged — this stage deletes refs and lands nothing. No branch carrying a `+` commit
is deleted. Each deleted ref's tip is preserved as an archive/<branch> tag pushed BEFORE the
deletion: patch-id equivalence means main carries an equivalent patch, not the same object, so
grant-merge-verbs' 99d8a49 becomes unreachable and GC-eligible the moment its ref goes. The
content survives without the tag; the commit does not.
subject.material:
Three remote refs: grant-merge-verbs, whose single commit 99d8a49 marks `=` against the
equivalent 7fe9a4d on main; and judge-import-blindness and solved-marker-007, each measured at
zero commits ahead of main and each absent from the brief's fifteen-branch inventory.
subject.result:
The three refs whose commits all have equivalent patches on main — grant-merge-verbs, plus the
two zero-ahead refs the brief's inventory omits — no longer exist on origin, and the ledger
records for each the command whose output licensed the deletion. The remaining ref namespace
contains only branches with genuinely unique content.

stages.knowledge:
That /Users/the0/claude-agent-instructions-grant is a linked worktree holding
reply-register-calques, so deleting that branch requires releasing the worktree first; that
land-branch.py removes a branch's worktree as part of landing; and that each landing moves main

means.means: git rebase in the isolated worktree; scripts/land-branch.py; python3 -m pytest; scripts/verify-all.sh
means.method:
The branches are handled ONE AT A TIME, each rebased, tested and landed to completion before
the next is started, so a failure is attributable to a single branch rather than to a batch.
Ordering runs from the narrowest file surface to the widest, so the cheapest evidence about how
badly main has drifted arrives first and can inform whether the wider ones are worth
attempting. Any branch whose rebase conflicts beyond straightforward resolution, or whose
rebased state regresses the baseline, is WITHDRAWN to file-as-task rather than forced — the
group's cheapness is its justification, and a branch that stops being cheap has left the
group. reply-register-calques is additionally checked out in a second worktree, which must be
released before its ref can be deleted. Each push to main is separately put to the user.
means.procedure:
1. Order the six by touched-file count: reply-register-calques and si/outcome-format-labels-ui-link (1), si/baseline-diff-granularity (4), de448-planner-plan-file-split, si/lang-agnostic-judge (18), host-isolated-spawn (28).
2. For each in turn: branch from the remote ref in the isolated worktree, rebase onto current main.
3. If the rebase conflicts beyond straightforward resolution, mark the branch file-as-task and move to the next.
4. Run the suite and verify-all.sh; compare the failure set against the baseline record.
5. Run land-branch.py --check, put the push to the user, and land on approval.
6. For reply-register-calques, release the /Users/the0/claude-agent-instructions-grant worktree before its ref is deleted.
7. Record the outcome and the resulting main SHA in the ledger row before starting the next branch.

stages.preconditions: A landing has already been performed and verified in stage 4, so the rebase-test-gate-land sequence is known to work in this repository before it is applied six more times.

principle.derivation:
These six are grouped for one reason: one commit each on a narrow surface, so the expected
rebase cost is small and a batch amortizes the setup. That reason is a prediction about the
rebase, not a property of the branch — and main has moved substantially since all six were
cut, so some prediction in the group will be wrong. If a branch that turns out to need

means.means: git rebase; scripts/gen_crutch_registry.py; scripts/land-branch.py; python3 -m pytest
means.method:
The two branches land SEQUENTIALLY in age order — the older, larger followup branch first,
then heredoc-body-spans rebased onto the result — because they are independent edits to one
subsystem and the younger branch's four commits are the ones that must be reconciled against
an already-reconciled base rather than the reverse. scripts/crutch_registry.toml is a
GENERATED artifact of scripts/gen_crutch_registry.py: its conflicts are resolved by
regenerating it from the merged tree, never by merging its hunks, because a hand-merged
generated file records a state its generator would not produce and the next regeneration
silently reverts the merge. The guard under change is the mechanism that protects the
canonical checkout, so its own tests are the acceptance evidence and are run against the
merged result, not merely against each branch.
means.procedure:
1. Rebase followup/guard-and-enumerate-residuals onto current main in the isolated worktree, taking main's side on crutch_registry.toml conflicts.
2. Regenerate the registry with scripts/gen_crutch_registry.py, run it a second time and confirm the artifact is byte-identical, then commit it. The second run is the determinism check the resolution rests on: if regeneration is not a function of the tree alone, resolving a conflict by regenerating is not a resolution and the divergence is a difficulty to declare rather than commit.
3. Run the guard and lexer test files, then the whole suite; compare against the baseline record.
4. Land it through land-branch.py behind a user gate.
5. Rebase heredoc-body-spans onto the new main, reconciling its shell_tokens.py and hook-guard-canon-readonly.py changes against the just-landed versions.
6. Regenerate the registry again and re-run the same tests.
7. Land it behind its own user gate, and record both outcomes in the ledger.

stages.preconditions: The six single-commit branches are disposed, so this stage's conflict resolution happens against a main that has stopped moving for reasons unrelated to this subsystem.

principle.derivation:
Four of the branches to be landed all modify this one file, so conflicts in it are certain
rather than possible, and at roughly 19500 lines a hand resolution is both expensive and
unreviewable. The file has a generator in the same tree, which means its correct content is a
FUNCTION of the merged source rather than a merge of two prior contents — so the merge
operation is not merely costly but ill-defined: any hand-resolved version that differs from
the generator's output is wrong by construction and will be silently overwritten the next time
anyone regenerates. Regeneration is therefore both the cheaper and the only correct
resolution.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if the registry turns out to carry hand-maintained content the generator does not
reproduce — a manually-curated section or a committed ground annotation — in which case
regeneration would destroy it and the conflict needs a real merge of the curated part.
principle.source: Measured this session: scripts/crutch_registry.toml appears in the touched-file set of followup/guard-and-enumerate-residuals, heredoc-body-spans, perm-self-grant and si/differential-verify, and scripts/gen_crutch_registry.py is its generator, itself modified on the followup branch.
principle.statement: A conflict in a generated file is resolved by re-running its generator, because a hand-merged artifact encodes a state its generator would not produce and the next regeneration discards the merge.

means.means: git log --cherry-mark; git diff; git rebase --dry-run equivalents; curl against api.github.com with the token in ~/.github-token; scripts/file-difficulty.py
means.method:
Each branch is adjudicated on three questions answered in order, stopping at the first that
decides it: is its purpose still live given what main has since gained; is its unique content
recoverable as a rebase at proportionate cost; and does landing it now serve a filed need. A
branch that fails any of these becomes file-as-task with the reasoning recorded — filing is a
real disposition here, not a euphemism for abandonment, and the filed task must carry enough
detail that the work is recoverable without re-deriving it from the diff. org-neutralize-core
is adjudicated as its five residual commits rather than as a branch, since 38 of its 43 already
landed and treating it whole would mis-state both its cost and its value. Where a branch's work
overlaps a filed public issue, that issue is the place the task is filed against rather than a
new one.
means.procedure:
1. For each of the five, re-run the patch-id pass against current main — several landings have moved it since stage 2.
2. Read each branch's unique commits and summarize what is on it that main lacks.
3. Attempt a rebase onto current main in a scratch branch to measure conflict cost without committing to landing.
4. Decide land or file-as-task per branch against the three questions.
5. For a land decision, follow the stage 4 sequence: test, --check, user gate, land.
6. For a file-as-task decision, file against the existing public issue where one matches, else create one carrying the branch name, its unique commits and the rebase cost measured in step 3.
7. Record the adjudication and its evidence in each ledger row.

stages.preconditions: The cheap and mid-cost branches are disposed, so the effort spent here is not competing with landings that would have moved main underneath it.

principle.derivation:
Reading the branch whole gives 43 commits and 221 files, which prices it as the largest item in
the backlog and would justify either a major effort or an abandonment. Reading its residual
gives five commits, which is comparable to the singletons in stage 6. Both figures describe the
same ref, and the decision they support is opposite — so pricing by branch rather than by
residual does not merely lose precision, it inverts the disposition. The same correction
applies to bench-v2/spawn-cost-ledger, priced at 7 commits but carrying 6 unique.
principle.refutation:
Refuted where a branch's residual commits depend on its landed ones in a way that makes them
unrebasable in isolation — then the residual cannot be lifted alone and the branch's real cost
is closer to its whole size after all.
principle.source: Measured this session: org-neutralize-core shows 43 commits and 221 files against main, of which the cherry-mark pass marks 38 `=` and only 5 `+`.
principle.statement: A branch's cost and value are properties of its unique commits, not of the branch, so a partially-landed branch is adjudicated as its residual rather than as its whole.

means.means: curl against api.github.com with the token in ~/.github-token for creating, commenting and closing; git ls-remote --heads origin; the stage 2 ledger
means.method:
The residue is enumerated from the LIVE remote rather than from the ledger, and the ledger is
then checked to account for what the enumeration found — the direction matters, because
enumerating from the ledger can only confirm rows that exist and is blind to a branch nobody
wrote a row for. Every remaining branch gets a task reference recorded in its row; a branch on
origin with no filed task is the precise failure this stage exists to prevent, since it is
indistinguishable from the state the whole task set out to end.
means.procedure:
1. Enumerate live remote branches with git ls-remote --heads origin.
2. Subtract main; for each remaining branch, look up its ledger row.
3. For any branch with no row, or a row lacking a task reference, file the task and record the reference.
4. For any branch whose row says land or discard yet which still exists on origin, re-open the discrepancy as a difficulty rather than editing the row to match.
5. Re-read the ledger and confirm every file-as-task row carries a reference.
6. Collect every issue whose reconciliation verdict says its fix has now landed and which is still open, and put them to the user as ONE batched gate showing each closing comment's text; on approval close them and record each closure in the issues record's fourth column. Batched rather than per-issue because user attention is an optimization axis and the decision is the same decision ten times over.

stages.preconditions: Every branch has received a disposition in stages 4-8, so this stage is accounting for decisions already made rather than making the last of them.

principle.derivation:
This plan's criterion is universal over branches. The instances this task touched are recorded
in the ledger, so a ledger-driven check can confirm each recorded disposition but is
structurally unable to detect a branch that was never recorded — the very case the brief
already exhibited by omitting judge-import-blindness and solved-marker-007 from a table of
fifteen. Enumerating from git ls-remote makes the remote, not the record of our own work, the
authority on what exists, which is the only direction in which an omission shows up.
principle.refutation:
Refuted if branches can be created on origin by other actors during the task, since then even
a live enumeration is a snapshot and completeness holds only as of its instant rather than
durably.

principle.statement: A universally-quantified done criterion is established by enumerating its domain from the authority that defines it, plus a negative end-state check — never by inspecting the instances that were acted on.

questions.question: Is gen_crutch_registry.py's output a function of the tree alone, as resolving a conflict by regeneration requires?
questions.risk: If the generator reads anything outside the tree, the second run differs and stage 7 declares a difficulty instead of committing — the failure is loud and costs one diagnosis rather than a silently wrong registry on main.

questions.basis: A branch appearing between stage 2 and stage 9 is treated the same way regardless of who pushed it: stage 9 files a task for it and records the reference. Filing a task for someone else's branch is harmless and leaves the ref untouched, since stage 9 deletes nothing.
questions.own_research: Read stage 9's method and step 4, and checked the repository's collaborator situation from the brief: this is a single-author fleet repository, so a branch appearing between stage 2 and stage 9 is far more likely one of ours pushed mid-flight than a third party's.
questions.question: If a branch appears on origin after stage 2's enumeration because another actor pushed it, does stage 9's file-as-task treatment apply to it?
questions.risk: A third party's branch acquires a task nobody asked for — noise, not damage, and stage 9's report-rather-than-edit rule surfaces it for a human to read.

questions.basis: The token makes a missing gate visible as a missing marker, and the actual proof lives in the session transcript and the engine history, which the user can read and the executor cannot rewrite.
questions.own_research: Read stage 4 step 8 and stage 9's control: the token is a marker inside an artifact the executor writes, so it cannot itself prove a gate was held. The independent trail is outside the plan — the AskUserQuestion call in the session transcript and the engine's own history event for the approval — and the plan's control checks that the marker is present rather than that the gate happened.
questions.question: The gate:approved token is written by the same executor that asked for the approval — what independently records that the user actually approved?
questions.risk: An executor could write the token without holding the gate; no artifact inside the plan can detect that, which is a ceiling of a self-recorded control rather than a defect this plan can close.

questions.basis: A hunk where the two directives genuinely contradict is one the stage's own refutation classifies as an unresolvable rebase, so the exit is withdrawal to file-as-task rather than a precedence rule; final_check 3 accepts that outcome.
questions.own_research: Read stage 4's method, its refutation clause and final_check 3: the stage already provides for a rebase that cannot be resolved (withdraw to file-as-task) and the final check accepts either disjunct of R5, so a genuinely conflicting hunk has a licensed exit that does not require guessing a precedence.
questions.question: When a single hunk in the rebase requires both favouring main's newer structure and preserving the emphasis-tolerance behaviour, which directive takes precedence?
questions.risk: The executor silently prefers one directive and lands a fix whose meaning main's newer structure has already changed, with the suite too coarse to notice.

questions.answer: Yes, if the script is invoked from anywhere other than the isolated worktree itself; the plan now requires the invocation cwd to be inside that worktree at stage 4 step 7, and stages 6 and 7 point at that step.
questions.derivation: The guard returns early only when realpath(worktree-holding-the-branch) equals realpath(repo_root), so equality is the only invocation that cannot remove the plan's own working tree.
questions.own_research: Read _worktree_for_branch and _cleanup_local_branch in scripts/land-branch.py (lines 158-215): the script locates whatever linked worktree has the landed branch checked out and runs git worktree remove on it, sparing it only when its realpath equals the invocation repo's realpath. Every landing stage rebases the branch inside the isolated worktree, so that worktree is the one holding the branch and an invocation from the canonical checkout would remove it mid-plan.
questions.question: Since land-branch.py removes the landed branch's linked worktree, can landing delete the stage-1 isolated worktree that stages 5-9 still depend on?

questions.basis: The scratch-branch rebase in step 3 turns the cost into an observation before any commitment, and the alternative to landing is file-as-task rather than abandonment, so an over-strict or over-generous reading costs a deferral, not a loss.
questions.own_research: Read stage 8's method and procedure step 3: the stage measures conflict cost by attempting the rebase on a scratch branch before committing to landing, so the judgement is made against a measurement rather than an estimate. No numeric threshold exists anywhere in the plan or the repository's tooling.
questions.question: What decides that a rebase's conflict cost is proportionate rather than not, and what evidence establishes that a branch's original purpose is still live?
questions.risk: An expensive rebase is attempted because proportionate was read generously, spending the heavyweight stage's budget on one branch.

questions.basis: Measured: the red set is exactly one test, and stage 1 records the full set by node id, so a discrepancy surfaces at stage 1 rather than at final verification. Deselecting by name is deliberate — it makes a rename show up as RED instead of silently widening the tolerance.
questions.own_research: Ran the full suite this session: 4660 passed, 3 skipped, 1 failed, the single red being test_hook_wiring.py::test_an_unsearchable_chain_member_is_unaccounted_for_not_absent. Read stage 1 procedure step 5, which records EVERY failing node id on its own known_red line, and stage 1's control, which requires at least one such line, so a larger red set is visible in the pinned baseline long before final_check 2 runs.
questions.question: final_check 2 deselects one known-red test by name; if stage 1 measures more than one known red, who widens the exclusion and does the done criterion still hold?
questions.risk: If the red set grows mid-plan, final_check 2 fails for a reason unrelated to regression and the deselection has to be widened by hand, which is a false FAILED rather than a missed one.

questions.basis: Stage 3 records candidates per issue and stage 9 step 6 now demands all of them have landed, so a partially-landed fix cannot mark an issue closable; the closing itself is a user gate that shows each comment's exact text.
questions.own_research: Read stage 3's method against the new stage 9 step 6: the mapping matters because step 6 derives a landed token from the ledger rows of the branches named in an issue's candidate column. I closed the worst case in the plan itself — step 6 requires every candidate branch on a row to have landed before the row can read as closable — and stage 3's method already requires a fix to be complete and tested before it may contradict a public claim.
questions.question: When a branch's touched files match more than one open issue, or an issue's defect spans files touched by more than one branch, which candidate becomes the branch recorded for that issue?
questions.risk: Two issues sharing one branch could both be marked landed when only one issue's defect surface was actually fixed, leaving the user's reading of the closing comment as the last check.

questions.answer: This session owns it; releasing it is safe and does not strand another session's work.
questions.derivation: A no-live-process foothold does not prove absence of an owner, so ownership has to come from the durable session record rather than from ps; the edit log is that record and it names only this session.
questions.own_research: Ran git worktree list (the worktree sits at 2b5fb27 on reply-register-calques) and grepped the agentctl edit log for that path: every write to it carries session_id 4597c2b0-b94e-463b-901c-6f30f60677f9, this session, from the grant-merge-verbs work earlier today. No other session id appears against it.
questions.question: Who owns the second worktree /Users/the0/claude-agent-instructions-grant that holds reply-register-calques, and is releasing it safe?

questions.answer: Public is the right destination for Core-tier content, but only after scripts/check-org-neutral.py passes on the body; anything it flags is split by tier instead of published, which both stages now say.
questions.derivation: Publishing is not reversible by deletion once indexed, so the check belongs before the post rather than after it.
questions.own_research: Checked that scripts/check-org-neutral.py exists in this repository and that the standing rule for this tracker is that the Core venue is public and every issue body passes that check before publication. The plan did not invoke it, so I added the check to stage 8 step 6 and stage 9 step 3 rather than leaving the obligation implicit.
questions.question: Is the public GitHub tracker the right destination for every file-as-task disposition, given some branch content may be org-internal?
questions.source: scripts/check-org-neutral.py present in the repository; the Core-venue-is-public rule in memory-global/leaves/instruction-dev-queues.md.

questions.basis: A flaky red produces a set difference at a later stage, which is a false FAILED routed into the difficulty cycle rather than a silent pass; the baseline is a comparison base, not an authority that can hide a regression.
questions.own_research: Ran the suite once this session (4660 passed, 3 skipped, 1 failed) and read stage 1's procedure: the baseline records every failing node id, and every later stage compares its failure SET against that file rather than a count, so a flake shows up as a set difference.
questions.question: What if the suite proves non-deterministic at the pinned SHA, given every later regression judgement rests on this one baseline?
questions.risk: A flaky test that happens to pass during the baseline run and fail later costs one diagnosis cycle per occurrence.
